citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: every family of nonempty sets has a choice function. It is assumed for the conditional-expectation and Doob interfaces used here.

citations.quote:
A **discrete filtered probability space** is $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0},P)$, where $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ is a probability space [[def-probability-measure]], each $\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra on $\Omega$ [[def-sigma-algebra]], and $\mathcal F_n\subseteq\mathcal F_{n+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$. The sequence $(\mathcal F_n)$ is a **filtration**. Time starts at zero. Neither completeness nor triviality of $\mathcal F_0$ is required.

Restriction of $P$ to $\mathcal F_n$ has total mass one and is countably additive: a disjoint sequence in $\mathcal F_n$ is also such a sequence in $\mathcal F$, with the same union and the same values of $P$. Thus each restriction is a probability measure. This specifies a structure and uses no choice principle. Real-valued processes will be the default.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]: $\mathcal F_k\subseteq\mathcal F_{k+1}\subseteq\mathcal F$.

citations.quote:
On a filtered probability space [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]], a **real stochastic process** is a sequence $(X_n)_{n\in\mathbb N_0}$ of real random variables [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] on the same space. It is **adapted** when $X_n^{-1}(B)\in\mathcal F_n$ for every $n$ and every real Borel set $B$. It is **integrable** when $E|X_n|<\infty$ for every $n$, using [[def-expectation-of-a-nonnegative-or-integrable-random-variable]].

An integrable adapted process satisfies both conditions at each fixed time. Integrability here does not mean $\sup_nE|X_n|<\infty$: the deterministic process $X_n=n$ has $E|X_n|=n<\infty$ at every time but unbounded supremum. Measurability and finiteness of each integral are separate requirements. No versions, limits or choices are selected.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]: adaptedness means $\mathcal F_k$-measurability at time $k$, and integrability means finite expectation of the absolute value at every fixed time.

citations.quote:
Assume AC for the supplied existence theorem. Write $E[X\mid\mathcal G]$ for the unique class in $L^1(\Omega,\mathcal G,P|_{\mathcal G})$ consisting of conditional-expectation versions of $X$. A chosen real $\mathcal G$-measurable representative is a **version**. Equalities and inequalities involving these classes mean almost-sure equalities and inequalities.

Existence is [[thm-conditional-expectation-exists-by-radon-nikodym]] and uniqueness is [[lem-conditional-expectation-is-unique-almost-surely]], applied to [[def-conditional-expectation-given-a-sigma-algebra]]. The quotient is [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]. If $X=X^{\ast}$ almost surely, [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]] gives identical event integrals, so the output class is independent of the input representative. The [[def-axiom-of-choice]] assumption is inherited from RN existence.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]: under AC, conditional expectations exist as almost-sure classes; inequalities and equalities between them are interpreted almost surely.

citations.quote: Assume AC. If $X$ is a submartingale with $C:=\sup_n\mathbb E[X_n^+]<\infty$, then there is an integrable finite random variable $X_\infty$ such that $X_n\to X_\infty$ almost surely.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-doob-submartingale-convergence]]: under AC, a submartingale $Y_k$ with $\sup_k\mathbb E[Y_k^+]<\infty$ has a finite integrable almost-sure limit.

citations.quote:
For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-real-exponential-function-and-e]]: $\exp(t)=\sum_{n\ge0}t^n/n!$, so $\exp(0)=1$.

citations.quote:
The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-derivative-of-exponential]]: $\exp'(t)=\exp(t)$.

citations.quote: The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-exponential-is-strictly-increasing]]: $\exp$ is increasing on $\mathbb R$.

citations.quote:
Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
citations.use_explanation: [[cor-mean-value-theorem]]: for a function continuous on $[u,v]$ and differentiable on $(u,v)$, some $w\in(u,v)$ satisfies $g(v)-g(u)=g'(w)(v-u)$.

citations.quote:
For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-exponential-addition-formula]]: $\exp(s+t)=\exp(s)\exp(t)$.

citations.quote:
Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty set of reals bounded above has a least upper bound.

citations.quote: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. Equivalently (property form): if a property $P$ satisfies $P(0)$ and ($P(n) \Rightarrow P(\sigma(n))$) for all $n$, then $P(n)$ holds for all $n \in \mathbb{N}$. This is the induction principle, the basis of proof by induction.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-induction-principle]]: a property true at $0$ and inherited by each successor holds for every natural index.

citations.quote: Assume AC for existence. For real $X,Y\in L^1(P)$ and $a,b\in\mathbb R$, $E[aX+bY\mid\mathcal G]=aE[X\mid\mathcal G]+bE[Y\mid\mathcal G]$. Conditional expectation is positive, preserves order and constants, satisfies $E(E[X\mid\mathcal G])=EX$, and $|E[X\mid\mathcal G]|\le E[|X|\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. Also $X<Y$ almost surely implies $E[X\mid\mathcal G]<E[Y\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-basic-algebra-and-order-properties-of-conditional-expectation]] supplies conditional linearity and preservation of constants.

citations.quote: Assume AC for existence. If $X\in L^1(P)$ and $Z$ is bounded real $\mathcal G$-measurable, then $E[ZX\mid\mathcal G]=ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ almost surely. The identity also holds for finite real $\mathcal G$-measurable $Z$ whenever $ZX$ and $ZE[X\mid\mathcal G]$ are integrable. In fact $X,ZX\in L^1$ imply the latter integrability.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]] allows deterministic factors and integrable filtration-measurable finite sums to pass through conditional expectation when the products are integrable.

derivations.claim: Define $A_0=1$, $A_{k+1}=A_k(1+a_k)$, and $T_k=\sum_{j\ge k}c_j/A_{j+1}$. Then $A_k\ge1$. For $t>0$, [F8] applied to $\exp$ on $[0,t]$ gives $\exp(t)-1=t\exp(w)$ for some $w\in(0,t)$; by [F5] and [F7], $\exp(w)\ge1$, so $1+t\le\exp(t)$, with equality at $t=0$. Repeated use of [F9] now gives $A_k\le\exp(\sum_{j<k}a_j)\le\exp(\sum_{j\ge0}a_j)$. Thus $A_k$ is nondecreasing and bounded. Let $A_\infty=\sup_k A_k$, which exists by [F10]; for every $\varepsilon>0$, some $n$ has $A_n>A_\infty-\varepsilon$, and then $A_\infty-\varepsilon<A_n\le A_k\le A_\infty$ for all $k\ge n$, so $A_k\to A_\infty\ge1$. If $C_m=\sum_{j<m}c_j$ and $C_\infty=\sup_m C_m$, then for every $\varepsilon>0$ some $m$ has $C_m>C_\infty-\varepsilon$; for $k\ge m$, $0\le T_k\le C_\infty-C_k\le C_\infty-C_m<\varepsilon$. Thus $T_k\to0$. [A1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F9, F10, F11, given, choose, algebra, induction]

Put $Z_k=X_k/A_k+T_k$. Each $Z_k$ is nonnegative, adapted, and integrable by [F1]–[F3]. By [F12], division by the positive deterministic $A_{k+1}$ and addition of the deterministic $T_{k+1}$ commute with conditional expectation. Since $A_{k+1}=A_k(1+a_k)$ and $T_k=c_k/A_{k+1}+T_{k+1}$, the given conditional inequality yields $\mathbb E[Z_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le ((1+a_k)X_k-b_k+c_k)/A_{k+1}+T_{k+1}=Z_k-b_k/A_{k+1}$. Hence $-Z_k$ is an integrable adapted submartingale with zero positive-part expectation. [F12] and [F4] give the finite almost-sure limit.

Define $S_k=\sum_{j<k}b_j/A_{j+1}$ and $W_k=Z_k+S_k$. Each summand is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable by the filtration inclusion and integrable; [F12] with the constant input 1 gives $\mathbb E[S_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=S_k$. Linearity in [F12] and step 2.1 give $\mathbb E[W_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le W_k$. Thus $-W_k$ is a submartingale with zero positive-part expectation, so [F4] gives a finite almost-sure limit for $W_k$. The increasing partial sums $S_k\le W_k$ therefore have a finite limit.

From $1\le A_{j+1}\le A_\infty$, step 3.1 implies $\sum_j b_j\le A_\infty\sum_j b_j/A_{j+1}<\infty$ almost surely. By definition, $X_k=A_k(Z_k-T_k)$; step 1.1 gives $A_k\to A_\infty$ and $T_k\to0$, and step 2.1 gives convergence of $Z_k$. Therefore $X_k$ converges to a finite nonnegative limit and the asserted decrement sum is finite. [step 1.1, step 2.1, step 3.1, algebra] ∎

citations.quote:
Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]]: $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k$, $x_k$ is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable, $G_k$ is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable, and vector conditional expectations are coordinatewise almost-sure classes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ be a discrete filtered probability space. Let $X_k$ be nonnegative, adapted, and integrable for every $k$. Let $a_k,c_k$ be deterministic nonnegative sequences with finite sums, and let $b_k$ be nonnegative, $\mathcal F_k$-measurable, and integrable. If
$$\mathbb E[X_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le(1+a_k)X_k-b_k+c_k\quad\text{almost surely for every }k,$$
then $X_k$ converges almost surely to a finite nonnegative random variable and $\sum_{k\ge0}b_k<\infty$ almost surely.
citations.use_explanation: [[lem-robbins-siegmund-almost-supermartingale]]: if $V_k$ is nonnegative adapted integrable and $\mathbb E[V_{k+1}\mid\mathcal F_k]\le V_k-b_k+c_k$ with $b_k\ge0$ predictable and $\sum c_k<\infty$, then $V_k$ converges almost surely and $\sum b_k<\infty$ almost surely.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]: $\|u\|_2^2=\langle u,u\rangle$ and the real inner product is symmetric.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

derivations.claim: Write $V_k=\|x_k-x^\ast\|_2^2$. Young’s inequality and [F6] bound the squared-update cross term, giving $V_{k+1}\le(1+\mu\alpha_k)V_k+(\alpha_k/\mu+\alpha_k^2)\|G_k\|_2^2$. [F4] and the conditional second-moment bound give $\mathbb E\|G_k\|_2^2\le M^2$. The conditional variance identity in [F1] gives $\mathbb E\|h(x_k)\|_2^2\le M^2$. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and

   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x_0\in C$. The Euclidean projection $P_C(y)$ is the unique nearest point to $y$ in $C$; its existence and equivalence with the proximal map of the indicator of $C$ are supplied by [[lem-prox-indicator-is-euclidean-projection]]. The indicator is zero on $C$ and $+\infty$ off $C$, as defined in [[def-indicator-function-of-closed-convex-set]]. For the filtration-adapted oracle of [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]], projected SGD takes, at each iteration $k$:

1. form $y_k=x_k-\alpha_kG_k$;
2. set $x_{k+1}=P_C(y_k)$.

The output is the next iterate, which lies in $C$. The procedure has no failure branch because the projection exists uniquely for every $y_k\in\mathbb R^d$ under the stated conditions. Its nonexpansiveness is not part of this definition; it is supplied by the proximal-map theorem when used in proofs.

$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be open and convex, let $C\subseteq U$ be convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Suppose $f|_C$ is $\mu$-strongly convex in the strong-Jensen sense of [[def-strong-convex-composite-objective]], for $\mu>0$; explicitly, for $x,y\in C$ and $0<t<1$,
$$f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)-\frac\mu2t(1-t)\|x-y\|_2^2.$$

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac{\mu}{2}\|y-x\|_2^2,$$

Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC supplies the conditional-expectation classes.

citations.quote:
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be nonempty, closed, and convex, and let $x_0\in C$. The Euclidean projection $P_C(y)$ is the unique nearest point to $y$ in $C$; its existence and equivalence with the proximal map of the indicator of $C$ are supplied by [[lem-prox-indicator-is-euclidean-projection]]. The indicator is zero on $C$ and $+\infty$ off $C$, as defined in [[def-indicator-function-of-closed-convex-set]]. For the filtration-adapted oracle of [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]], projected SGD takes, at each iteration $k$:

1. form $y_k=x_k-\alpha_kG_k$;
2. set $x_{k+1}=P_C(y_k)$.

The output is the next iterate, which lies in $C$. The procedure has no failure branch because the projection exists uniquely for every $y_k\in\mathbb R^d$ under the stated conditions. Its nonexpansiveness is not part of this definition; it is supplied by the proximal-map theorem when used in proofs.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-projected-stochastic-gradient-update]]: $x_{k+1}=P_C(x_k-\alpha G_k)$.

citations.quote:
Let $g:\mathbb R^n\to(-\infty,+\infty]$ be proper, closed and convex in the epigraph convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, the set $\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)$ is a singleton. Its unique element $u$ satisfies the resolvent equivalence
$$u=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (v-u)/t\in\partial g(u).$$
For any $v_1,v_2$ and $u_i=\operatorname{prox}_{tg}(v_i)$,
$$\|u_1-u_2\|_2^2\le\langle u_1-u_2,v_1-v_2\rangle.$$
In particular the proximal map is nonexpansive.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolvent-firm-nonexpansive]]: the proximal map is nonexpansive.

citations.quote: Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be nonempty, closed and convex. Its indicator $\iota_C$ is proper, closed and convex in the convention of [[def-proper-closed-convex-function-on-rn]]. For every $t>0$ and $v\in\mathbb R^n$, $\operatorname{prox}_{t\iota_C}(v)$ is the singleton consisting of the unique nearest point in $C$ to $v$.
citations.use_explanation: [[lem-prox-indicator-is-euclidean-projection]]: the proximal map of $\iota_C$ is $P_C$, and it fixes every point of $C$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and convex, and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be differentiable. Then $f$ is convex if and only if

$$f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle\qquad(x,y\in U).$$

Equivalently, $\nabla f(x)$ is a subgradient at every $x$ ([[def-subgradient-and-subdifferential]], [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]]).
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-differentiable-convex-functions-and-gradient-inequality]]: for differentiable convex $f$, $f(y)\ge f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle$.

citations.quote:
Let $C\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be convex ([[def-convex-subset-of-euclidean-space]]). The function $f:C\to\mathbb R$ is convex when $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for all $x,y\in C$ and $t\in[0,1]$. The parameter interval is the closed interval of [[def-interval]].

It is strictly convex when the inequality is strict for distinct $x,y$ and $0<t<1$. No strict inequality is required at $t=0$ or $t=1$, where the two sides coincide. The empty set and a singleton support convex functions, and strict convexity on either is vacuous.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-convex-and-strictly-convex-functions-on-euclidean-sets]]: convexity means $f((1-t)x+ty)\le(1-t)f(x)+tf(y)$ for $t\in[0,1]$.

citations.quote: Let $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$. If $0 \in S$ and $\sigma(n) \in S$ whenever $n \in S$, then $S = \mathbb{N}$. citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Assume AC. For real $X\in L^2(P)$ define $\operatorname{Var}(X\mid\mathcal G)=E[(X-E[X\mid\mathcal G])^2\mid\mathcal G]$ as an almost-sure class. Its integrability, nonnegativity, representative independence and second-moment formula are justified by the following lemma.

The conditional class is [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], with [[def-axiom-of-choice]] inherited from existence. By [[cor-conditional-lp-contraction]], a version of the conditional mean is square integrable. The unbounded-factor rule [[thm-taking-out-what-is-known]] will apply to products whose integrability is verified in the well-definedness lemma, recorded under `justified_by`.

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and let $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$, with the Euclidean
inner product and the Euclidean norm as in [[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Then:

1. **Cauchy-Schwarz.**
   $$\lvert\langle x,y\rangle\rvert \;\le\; \lVert x\rVert_2\,\lVert y\rVert_2 ,$$
   with equality if and only if there is a pair $(\lambda,\mu) \ne (0,0)$ of
   reals with $\lambda x_k = \mu y_k$ for every $k < n$.
2. **$\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm on $\mathbb{R}^{n}$**
   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.
3. **Parallelogram law.**
   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

**Clause 1 is a citation, not a new proof.** The inequality and its equality case
are the published [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-finite]], stated there for two lists of
reals; all that happens below is that it is read in the vector notation of
[[def-euclidean-inner-product]]. Re-proving it here would put two proofs of one
statement in the library.
citations.use_explanation: [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]]: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|_2\|v\|_2$.

Let $F$ be an ordered field ([[def-ordered-field]]) and $S \subseteq F$.

- $u \in F$ is an **upper bound** of $S$ if $s \le u$ for all $s \in S$; $S$ is
  **bounded above** if it has an upper bound.
- $u \in F$ is a **least upper bound** (or **supremum**, $\sup S$) of $S$ if $u$
  is an upper bound of $S$ and $u \le u'$ for every upper bound $u'$ of $S$.

$F$ is a **complete ordered field** (equivalently, $F$ has the
**least-upper-bound property**, or is **Dedekind complete**) if every nonempty
$S \subseteq F$ that is bounded above has a least upper bound in $F$.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-complete-ordered-field]]: every nonempty set of reals bounded above has a supremum.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]] defines conditional unbiasedness as E[G_k|F_k]=grad f(x_k), coordinatewise almost surely.

derivations.claim: The pairwise distances in nonempty $C$ form a nonempty bounded set, so [F12] gives their supremum $D$. By [F10] and [F13], $\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2\le\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le G^2$. Since $x_k,x^\ast\in C$, their distance is at most $D$. [F4] and [F11] give $0\le f(x_k)-f(x^\ast)\le\langle\nabla f(x_k),x_k-x^\ast\rangle\le DG$, so the objective values are integrable.

The projection fixes $x^\ast$ by [F3] and is nonexpansive by [F2]. Expanding the projection estimate, then conditioning using [F1], [F7], and the unbiasedness identity [F13], gives $\mathbb E[\|x_{k+1}-x^\ast\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le\|x_k-x^\ast\|_2^2-2\alpha(f(x_k)-f(x^\ast))+\alpha^2G^2$ by the convex gradient inequality [F4].

Take ordinary expectations in step 2.1 and sum for $k=0,\ldots,N-1$. The distance terms telescope, $\mathbb E\|x_N-x^\ast\|_2^2\ge0$, and $\|x_0-x^\ast\|_2\le D$, so $2\alpha\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E[f(x_k)-f(x^\ast)]\le D^2+N\alpha^2G^2$. [F7, step 2.1, given, algebra]

Convexity keeps $\bar x_N$ in $C$ and gives $f(\bar x_N)\le N^{-1}\sum_{k<N}f(x_k)$. To verify this finite Jensen inequality, induction starts with equality for one point; the step writes the $m$-point mean as $\frac{m-1}{m}$ times the $(m-1)$-point mean plus $\frac1m x_{m-1}$, then applies [F5]. Take expectations and use step 3.1 to get $\mathbb E[f(\bar x_N)-f(x^\ast)]\le\frac{D^2}{2\alpha N}+\frac{\alpha G^2}{2}$. [F5, F6, step 3.1, given, algebra, induction]

With $\alpha=D/(G\sqrt N)$, the two terms in step 4.1 are each $DG/(2\sqrt N)$, proving the stated bound. If $D=0$, $C$ is a singleton and $x_0=x^\ast$. If $G=0$, [F8] applied to each conditional moment and expectation-preservation in [F7] give $G_k=0$ almost surely for every fixed $k$. For each finite horizon, induction using [F6] shows all its iterates equal $x_0$ almost surely. Unbiasedness at $k=0$ gives $\nabla f(x_0)=0$, and [F4] makes $x_0$ a global minimizer. Thus the zero-case bound holds for every $N$. [A1, F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 4.1, given, algebra, induction] ∎

A **finite probability space** is a pair $(\Omega,w)$ consisting of a finite set $\Omega$ and a function $w:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ such that $w(\omega)\ge0$ for every $\omega\in\Omega$ and
$$\sum_{\omega\in\Omega}w(\omega)=1.$$
The elements of $\Omega$ are **outcomes**. Every subset $A\subseteq\Omega$ is an **event**, and its probability is
$$\mathbb P(A):=\sum_{\omega\in A}w(\omega).$$

An outcome of weight zero remains an outcome. Thus an event can be nonempty and still have probability zero.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-finite-probability-space-and-event]]: each of the two outcomes $Y=-1,1$ has weight $1/2$.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$ be a probability space.

- If $X:\Omega\to[0,+\infty]$ is measurable, its **expectation** is the
  extended-valued integral
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P\in[0,+\infty].$$
- If $X:\Omega\to\mathbb R$ or $X:\Omega\to\mathbb C$ is integrable in the sense
  of [[def-integrable-real-and-complex-functions-and-their-integrals]], its
  **expectation** is again
  $$\mathbb E[X]:=\int_\Omega X\,d\mathbb P,$$

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

   ([[def-norm-and-normed-space]]), for **every** $n \in \mathbb{N}$; the metric
   it induces is $d_2$ of [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] whenever $n \ge 1$.

   $$\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} + \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2} \;=\; 2\lVert x\rVert_2^{2} + 2\lVert y\rVert_2^{2} .$$
4. **Polarisation.**
   $$\langle x,y\rangle \;=\; \tfrac14\Bigl(\lVert x+y\rVert_2^{2} - \lVert x-y\rVert_2^{2}\Bigr),$$
   so the inner product is recovered from the norm it induces.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-axiom-of-choice]]: AC is used by the conditional-expectation formulation of the bias-floor theorem.

citations.quote:
Fix a finite dimension $d\ge1$ and a discrete filtered probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_k)_{k\ge0},P)$ as in [[def-filtration-and-filtered-probability-space]]. A sequence $x_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an iterate process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable; a sequence $G_k:\Omega\to\mathbb R^d$ is an oracle process when each coordinate is $\mathcal F_{k+1}$-measurable. These are coordinatewise instances of [[def-random-element-and-real-random-variable]] and [[def-adapted-and-integrable-stochastic-process]]. Assume the coordinates used in a conditional moment are square-integrable.

For deterministic stepsizes $\alpha_k>0$, the unconstrained Robbins–Monro/SGD update is
$$x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha_kG_k.$$
For a differentiable objective $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$, the oracle is conditionally unbiased when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)$ coordinatewise almost surely; it has conditional bias $b_k$ when $\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k$. The conditional variance of a vector is the sum of the scalar conditional variances of its coordinates, using [[def-conditional-variance]]. By [[lem-conditional-variance-is-well-defined-and-has-the-second-moment-formula]], it satisfies
$$\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]=\|\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]\|_2^2+\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)$$
almost surely. All conditional expectations are coordinatewise instances of [[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]], whose existence assumes the [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. No independence across iterations is part of this definition.

The conditional second-moment bound $\mathbb E[\|G_k\|_2^2\mid\mathcal F_k]\le M_k^2$ and the conditional variance bound $\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$ are distinct hypotheses; the latter combines with conditional unbiasedness through the displayed identity.
citations.use_explanation: [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]]: the unconstrained update is $x_{k+1}=x_k-\alpha G_k$.

citations.quote:
Assume AC. Let $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R$ have $L$-Lipschitz gradient for $L>0$ and satisfy $f(x)\ge f_{\inf}$ for a real lower bound $f_{\inf}$. Run the unconstrained update of [[def-stochastic-gradient-oracle-and-unconstrained-update]] from square-integrable $x_0$ with deterministic steps $0<\alpha_k\le1/(4L)$. Suppose
$$\mathbb E[G_k\mid\mathcal F_k]=\nabla f(x_k)+b_k,\qquad
\|b_k\|_2\le\beta_k,\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(G_k\mid\mathcal F_k)\le\sigma_k^2$$
almost surely, where $b_k$ is $\mathcal F_k$-measurable and $\beta_k,\sigma_k$ are deterministic nonnegative bounds. For $N\ge1$ and $\Delta=\mathbb E f(x_0)-f_{\inf}<\infty$,
$$\frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2}{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\alpha_k}\le
\frac{2\Delta+2\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k\beta_k^2+2L\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\beta_k^2+L\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k^2\sigma_k^2}{\sum_{k<N}\alpha_k}.$$
In particular, for constant $\alpha,\beta,\sigma$ the uniform average is at most
$$\frac{2\Delta}{\alpha N}+\frac52\beta^2+L\alpha\sigma^2,$$
and therefore
$$\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\mathbb E\|\nabla f(x_k)\|_2^2\le\frac52\beta^2+L\alpha\sigma^2.$$
Decreasing steps retain the displayed weighted bias and noise sums.

citations.quote:
Let $r \in \mathbb{R}$ and let $r^k$ be the integer power ([[def-integer-power]]).

1. If $|r| < 1$ then $(r^k)$ is **null**, that is $r^k \to 0$
   ([[def-real-limit]]).
2. If $|r| > 1$ then $(|r|^k)$ **diverges to $+\infty$**
   ([[def-divergence-to-infinity]]).

Claim 2 is stated for $|r|^k$ and not for $r^k$ on purpose: for $r < -1$ the
terms $r^k$ alternate in sign and are unbounded, so they neither converge nor
diverge to $+\infty$; what is true of them is the statement about their absolute
values.

Both claims come from Bernoulli's inequality ([[lem-bernoulli-inequality]]) and
the Archimedean property. Nothing here needs the least-upper-bound property
except through [[thm-of-archimedean]] and [[cor-archimedean-reciprocal]].

citations.quote:
Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$. A natural number is a von Neumann natural, that is a set,
and $n = \{0, 1, \dots, n-1\}$ ([[def-natural-numbers]],
[[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]), so

$$\mathbb{R}^{n} \;=\; \{\, x \;:\; x \text{ is a function } n \to \mathbb{R} \,\}$$

is the function space of [[def-function-space]] at $F = \mathbb{R}$ and $X = n$,
a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$ under the pointwise operations
([[def-vector-space]]). We write $x_k := x(k)$ for $k < n$, and two elements of
$\mathbb{R}^{n}$ are equal exactly when they agree at every $k < n$. This is the
same set that [[lem-metrics-on-rn]] calls $\mathbb{R}^{n}$.

The **Euclidean inner product** of $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ is the real number

$$\langle x, y\rangle \;:=\; \sum_{k<n} x_k\,y_k ,$$

the finite sum of [[def-finite-sum]] applied to the list $k \mapsto x_k y_k$
(extended by $0$ beyond $n$, as every finite list in this library is). The
**Euclidean norm** of $x$ is

$$\lVert x\rVert_2 \;:=\; \sqrt{\langle x, x\rangle},$$

which is defined because $\langle x,x\rangle = \sum_{k<n} x_k^{2} \ge 0$ (a sum
of nonnegative terms, [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4 and
[[lem-of-square-positive]], the case $x_k = 0$ giving $x_k^2 = 0$ by
[[def-integer-power]]) and every nonnegative real has a unique nonnegative square
root ([[thm-of-square-roots]]).

### Both are defined for every $n$, including $n = 0$

At $n = 0$ the set $\mathbb{R}^{0}$ has exactly one element, the empty function,
and it is the zero vector space ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]] clause 5); the sum
above is the empty sum, so $\langle x,y\rangle = 0$ and $\lVert x\rVert_2 = 0$.
**This is the first place on this page where the two index regimes diverge, and
the divergence is deliberate.** The published metrics $d_1$, $d_2$, $d_\infty$ of
[[lem-metrics-on-rn]] are defined only for $n \ge 1$, because $d_\infty$ would
otherwise be a maximum over the empty index set; the algebra above needs no such
restriction. The boundary in this page runs between the algebra and the metric,
not where a reader would guess, and [[rem-rn-conventions-and-scope]] lists
exactly which items inherit $n \ge 1$.

### The algebra of the inner product

For all $x, y, z \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

1. **Symmetry.** $\langle x,y\rangle = \langle y,x\rangle$, since $x_ky_k = y_kx_k$
   termwise.
2. **Additivity in the first argument.**
   $\langle x + y, z\rangle = \langle x,z\rangle + \langle y,z\rangle$: the list
   $k \mapsto (x_k+y_k)z_k$ is the termwise sum of $k \mapsto x_kz_k$ and
   $k \mapsto y_kz_k$, so [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 1 applies.
3. **Homogeneity in the first argument.**
   $\langle \lambda x, y\rangle = \lambda\langle x,y\rangle$, by
   [[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 2.
4. **Bilinearity.** Clauses 2 and 3 together with symmetry give the same two laws
   in the second argument.
5. **Positive definiteness.** $\langle x,x\rangle \ge 0$, and
   $\langle x,x\rangle = 0$ if and only if $x = 0$. Indeed a vanishing sum of
   nonnegative terms has every term $0$ ([[lem-finite-sum-laws]] clause 4), so
   $x_k^{2} = 0$ for every $k < n$, and a nonzero real has a positive square
   ([[lem-of-square-positive]]), whence $x_k = 0$ for every $k < n$ and $x = 0$.
6. **Agreement with the published Euclidean metric.** For $n \ge 1$ and
   $x, y \in \mathbb{R}^{n}$,
   $\lVert x - y\rVert_2 = \sqrt{\sum_{k<n}(x_k-y_k)^{2}} = d_2(x,y)$, the two
   sides being the same expression ([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). In particular
   $\lVert x\rVert_2 = d_2(x, 0)$.

That $\lVert\cdot\rVert_2$ is a norm in the sense of [[def-norm-and-normed-space]]
is proved in [[thm-cauchy-schwarz-and-the-euclidean-norm]], where the triangle
inequality is obtained from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; it is not assumed
here.

Throughout, $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]), neighbourhoods are those of
[[def-neighbourhood-r]] and limit points those of [[def-limit-point-r]].

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $f : A \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $c \in A$ be a
**limit point of $A$**. The **difference quotient of $f$ at $c$** is the function

$$q_{f,c} : A \setminus \{c\} \to \mathbb{R}, \qquad q_{f,c}(x) := \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

The division is legitimate at every point of the domain, since $x \ne c$ gives
$x - c \ne 0$.

**The point $c$ is a limit point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, not merely of $A$.**
For every real $\varepsilon > 0$ the punctured neighbourhood
$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c)$ omits $c$, so

$$N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap A \;=\; N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(c) \cap (A \setminus \{c\}) ,$$

and the left-hand side is nonempty because $c$ is a limit point of $A$. So
$q_{f,c}$ is a function on a set having $c$ as a limit point, and
$\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x)$ is a notion that [[def-function-limit]] defines.

$f$ is **differentiable at $c$** when that limit exists, and then the
**derivative of $f$ at $c$** is

$$f'(c) \;:=\; \lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) \;=\; \lim_{x \to c} \frac{f(x) - f(c)}{x - c} .$$

**Two obligations are carried by that notation, and both are discharged here.**

1. **Uniqueness.** Writing $f'(c)$ treats the right-hand side as a name for a
   single real number. That is legitimate: $c$ is a limit point of the domain
   $A \setminus \{c\}$ of $q_{f,c}$, so at most one real can satisfy the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ condition, by [[lem-function-limit-unique]] applied to
   $q_{f,c}$. Two reals both meeting the condition are therefore equal, and the
   symbol denotes.
2. **Meaningfulness.** The hypothesis that $c$ is a limit point of $A$ is not
   decoration. At an **isolated** point of $A$ the punctured condition
   $0 < |x - c| < \delta$ is met by no point of the domain at all, so the
   $\varepsilon$-$\delta$ formula is satisfied vacuously by *every* real at
   once; this is why [[def-function-limit]] leaves the limit undefined there,
   and it is why this library defines $f'(c)$ only at a limit point of $A$. At
   an isolated point of its domain a function is neither differentiable nor
   non-differentiable here: the question is not posed.

**The limit sees only $A \setminus \{c\}$, so how the difference quotient is
extended to $c$ is irrelevant.** Let $Q : A \to \mathbb{R}$ agree with
$q_{f,c}$ at every point of $A \setminus \{c\}$, and let $L \in \mathbb{R}$.
Then $\lim_{x \to c} Q(x) = L$ if and only if $\lim_{x \to c} q_{f,c}(x) = L$.
Both conditions read: for every real $\varepsilon > 0$ there is a real
$\delta > 0$ such that every point $x$ of the relevant domain with
$0 < |x - c| < \delta$ satisfies $|{\cdot} - L| < \varepsilon$
([[def-function-limit]]). The clause $0 < |x - c|$ removes $x = c$ from both
quantifiers, so in both cases the points quantified over are exactly the
$x \in A \setminus \{c\}$ with $0 < |x - c| < \delta$, at which $Q$ and
$q_{f,c}$ take the same value. The two conditions are the same condition.

**Differentiability on a set.** For $S \subseteq A$, $f$ is **differentiable on
$S$** when it is differentiable at every $c \in S$; implicit in that phrase is
that every point of $S$ is a limit point of $A$. $f$ is **differentiable** when
it is differentiable on the whole of $A$.

**Restriction of the domain.** Let $B \subseteq A$, let $c \in B$ and suppose
$c$ is a limit point of $B$. If $f$ is differentiable at $c$, then so is the
restriction $f|_B : B \to \mathbb{R}$, and

$$(f|_B)'(c) \;=\; f'(c) .$$

Indeed $B \setminus \{c\} \subseteq A \setminus \{c\}$; the displayed identity
of punctured neighbourhoods above, applied to $B$, shows that $c$ is a limit
point of $B \setminus \{c\}$; the difference quotient $q_{f|_B, c}$ is the
restriction of $q_{f,c}$ to $B \setminus \{c\}$, since $f|_B(c) = f(c)$; and
claim 2 of [[lem-limit-is-local]] carries the limit to that restriction.

**Every point of a nondegenerate interval is a limit point of it.** Let
$J \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ be order-convex ([[def-interval]]) with at least two
elements and let $p \in J$. Choose $q \in J$ with $q \ne p$, and let a real
$\varepsilon > 0$ be given. If $p < q$, put $y := p + \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ q - p\}$;
then $p < y$, and $y - p \le \tfrac{1}{2}(q-p) < q - p$, so $p < y < q$ and
order-convexity gives $y \in J$, while $0 < |y - p| < \varepsilon$. If $q < p$,
the point $y := p - \tfrac{1}{2}\min\{\varepsilon,\ p - q\}$ serves in the same
way. So $N^{*}_{\varepsilon}(p) \cap J \ne \varnothing$ for every real
$\varepsilon > 0$, that is, $p$ is a limit point of $J$
([[def-limit-point-r]]).

Consequently, for $f$ defined on a nondegenerate interval $I$, the symbol
$f'(c)$ is meaningful at **every** $c \in I$, endpoints included. At an endpoint
the difference quotient is taken over the points of $I$ lying on the one side
that is available, so what other texts call a one-sided derivative is, here,
simply the derivative of $f$ on $I$.
